item.title: While Software Ate the World, This Company Ate Its Own Software Business
item.dc:creator: TechNode Staff
item.description: Editor’s note: This article is republished from Jumpstart, a TechNode Group publication. In 2023, AI software was DataCanvas’s business. item.content:encoded:
Editor’s note: This article is republished from Jumpstart, a TechNode Group publication.

In 2023, AI software was DataCanvas’s business. By the first half of 2026, it was almost absent from its sales.

The change is unusually stark. AI foundational software services generated 76.5% of the Chinese company’s revenue in 2023. Three years later, their contribution had fallen to 0.1%.

This was more than an old division being overshadowed by a faster-growing one. Software-service revenue itself contracted—from RMB81.3 million in 2023 to less than RMB500,000 in the first six months of 2026. Meanwhile, total annual revenue climbed from RMB106.2 million in 2023 to RMB1.10 billion in 2025, a compound annual growth rate of 221.5%.

DataCanvas had built a different business.

The Beijing company, known in China as 九章云极, began redirecting its resources toward computing infrastructure in early 2023. It subsequently added cloud services, turning from a supplier of software tools into a company that helps assemble computing infrastructure and sells access to its capacity.

On September 29, 2026, it filed for a Hong Kong listing. The application opens a window onto that reinvention: a company founded more than a decade ago, approaching the public market with its original revenue engine effectively switched off.

Before the Servers

DataCanvas was established in 2013, long before generative AI made computing infrastructure a mainstream business story.

Its early proposition was to help organizations work with data and build machine-learning models. A visual modelling platform followed in 2014, with subsequent products extending across model development and deployment.

These tools addressed an awkward gap inside enterprises. Having data did not mean a company could readily turn it into a working model. Building a model did not mean it could be reliably incorporated into everyday operations.

DataCanvas offered software to bridge those steps. Its products helped customers prepare data, construct analytical workflows and put models to work.

But building the technology was not the same as finding a business.

In 2022, founder and chairman Fang Lei recalled that the team had spent its early years concentrating on code while underestimating the market. The founders were experienced engineers; understanding what customers would actually pay for took longer.

Banks became an important entry point. They had substantial data, established technology budgets and reasons to improve how information informed decisions. Working with such customers gave DataCanvas a commercial setting for its tools—and a clearer understanding of what it meant to sell them.

The company offered enterprises the means to develop and use machine learning. Customers still had to provide the computing environments in which those tools would operate.

That boundary would become the next business opportunity.

The Decision to Change the Business

By 2023, large AI models were making the machinery behind software much harder to ignore.

Customers needed substantial computing resources, coordinated across processors, networks and storage. They had to obtain that capacity, make the components work together and keep workloads running.

For DataCanvas, this opened a choice: continue selling software into those environments, or take responsibility for more of the infrastructure itself.

It chose the latter.

The company began providing computing infrastructure solutions in 2023 and signed its first project contract that September. These were larger assignments than delivering a standalone software platform. They involved designing the computing environment, procuring and integrating hardware, and deploying systems to support customers’ workloads.

DataCanvas redirected resources toward the new operation while progressively withdrawing from its original software-service business.

The commercial consequences appeared quickly. Infrastructure solutions generated RMB24.9 million in 2023. By 2025, they brought in just over RMB1 billion and accounted for 91.2% of total revenue.

The old business moved in the opposite direction. Its revenue fell in both 2024 and 2025.

This was the decisive break in DataCanvas’s history. Selling tools had given it a role inside customers’ technology operations. Delivering infrastructure made it responsible for more of the environment those operations depended on.

The company had moved closer to the machinery—and taken on a larger share of the work.

Build It, Then Keep It Running

The next step came when DataCanvas launched its cloud service in September 2024.

An infrastructure project helps a customer establish computing capacity. A cloud service lets customers access capacity without arranging an entire installation themselves.

For DataCanvas, that meant moving beyond project delivery toward an ongoing operating relationship.

The first cloud-service revenue was tiny: RMB196,000 in 2024. It rose to RMB77.6 million in 2025 and reached RMB153.8 million in the first half of 2026. By then, cloud services supplied 26.1% of revenue, alongside the 73.8% generated by infrastructure solutions.

Its cloud-service enterprise customer count increased from two in 2024 to 75 in 2025 and 84 in the first half of 2026.

That progression gives the reinvention two distinct stages. Infrastructure projects first established the scale of the new business. Cloud services then began changing how the company maintained and monetized its relationship with customers.

A completed installation could produce project revenue. Providing access to computing capacity created a reason for customers to keep buying.

The software company had become an infrastructure provider. It was now also becoming an operator.

What Survived the Reinvention

DataCanvas did not stop writing software when software services stopped driving its sales.

It introduced Alaya NeW OS in April 2024, placing a software control layer at the centre of its newer business. The system coordinates computing resources and the workloads using them. Its subsequent cloud platforms build on that foundation.

This is the revealing tension in the transformation. DataCanvas was withdrawing a way of selling software while retaining the engineering that made its new services work.

Previously, the platform was something a customer bought. Increasingly, it became the mechanism through which DataCanvas delivered another product: usable computing capacity.

The company also developed its own computing measurement unit, DCU, which it markets in China as “one degree of computing power,” echoing the everyday expression for a unit of electricity.

The idea is to make computing easier to measure and purchase across different resources, with charges linked to consumption. It expresses the company’s new ambition in practical terms: customers should be able to buy computing as a service without assembling every ingredient needed to produce it.

For DataCanvas, this offered a different answer to a question it had encountered early in its life: what should an enterprise buy from the company?

Its first answer was software that helped customers develop and deploy models. Its newer answer included the resources on which those models run.

The Price of Starting Again

Replacing a business can produce a spectacular growth chart. It also changes what growth costs.

DataCanvas reported an overall gross margin of 40.6% in 2023, falling to 11.7% in 2024 as infrastructure solutions became the dominant source of sales. The margin recovered to 17.4% in 2025 and 31% in the first half of 2026.

The initial decline shows the distance between the two businesses. An infrastructure contract can contain substantial hardware procurement and deployment work. A much larger order can therefore bring a much larger cost of delivery.

Operating computing services adds another set of demands. Capacity must be available when customers need it, supported by systems that allocate resources and keep workloads functioning. Winning an order is only part of the job.

DataCanvas combines arrangements with infrastructure owners and partners with investment of its own. Moving into computing delivery nevertheless brings equipment costs, capacity commitments and the continuing task of turning available resources into paying usage.

Profitability remains unfinished. Its adjusted net loss narrowed from RMB194.3 million in 2023 to RMB91.3 million in 2025, then to RMB14.9 million in the first half of 2026.

Its reported first-half loss was much larger, at RMB1.09 billion, principally because of RMB1.07 billion in fair-value changes in financial liabilities. That accounting charge explains most of the gap between the reported and adjusted figures.

DataCanvas has demonstrated that it can replace its old revenue. It is still establishing how much it can earn from the replacement.

Taking the New Company Public

The Hong Kong IPO arrives three years into the transformation.

DataCanvas plans to use the proceeds to strengthen research and development, expand computing resources for its data-centre projects, develop sales channels and support working capital. Hardware procurement forms part of the proposed capacity expansion.

Those plans extend the decision made in 2023. The company is seeking capital to deepen a business that has already reshaped its operations and revenue.

For prospective shareholders, the task is to understand what that business has become. DataCanvas carries the history and technical capabilities of a software company. Most of its revenue now comes from infrastructure delivery, while cloud operations account for a growing share.

Its founding identity no longer describes how it makes most of its money.

What makes DataCanvas distinctive is the extent of the choice it has already made. It spent a decade building tools for enterprises to use AI, then deliberately stepped away from selling those tools as its main business. In their place, it built the infrastructure and services needed to keep those systems running.

The revenue transformation is largely complete. The Hong Kong listing brings the next question into public view: whether the business DataCanvas chose to become can turn its reinvention into durable earnings.

item.title: Kling AI 4.0 suggests a shift in AI video competition from visual quality to directorial control
item.dc:creator: Jessie Wu
item.description: AI video generation is no longer just about producing a visually impressive clip. For creators looking to use AI to make short films, advertisements or even feature films, the harder questions are whether characters can remain consistent, whether shots can unfold as intended, and whether a video can tell a coherent story from beginning to […]
item.content:encoded:
AI video generation is no longer just about producing a visually impressive clip. For creators looking to use AI to make short films, advertisements or even feature films, the harder questions are whether characters can remain consistent, whether shots can unfold as intended, and whether a video can tell a coherent story from beginning to end.

Kling AI’s latest release, Kling 4.0, introduces features designed to tackle these challenges. The model update focuses on motion performance, creative control and longer-form storytelling.

Kling 4.0 supports native video generation of up to 30 seconds in a single generation, along with up to 15 multimodal reference assets and 10 keyframes, giving creators more control over characters, scenes, actions and camera movements. Rather than focusing solely on visual quality, these features reflect a broader effort to make AI video generation more consistent and easier to control.

From generating images to directing shots

AI video creation has traditionally relied heavily on text prompts. Creators describe the scenes they want, and the model generates the footage. However, complex camera movements, character actions and scene transitions can be difficult to control precisely. Even when individual shots look convincing, combining them can result in inconsistent character appearances or discontinuous actions.

Kling 4.0’s multimodal reference feature supports images, videos and audio as inputs, with up to 15 reference assets. Its keyframe feature supports up to 10 control points for planning character states, action changes and scene transitions.

The two features serve different purposes. Reference assets help the model understand how a video should look and feel, while keyframes allow creators to define how a story should unfold.

A Kling AI spokesperson told TechNode that these capabilities target two major challenges in AI video creation: creative control and narrative continuity. Text prompts alone can make it difficult to describe characters, settings, action rhythms and camera movements precisely.

Multimodal references and keyframes provide additional ways to guide the generation process, which helps creators exert greater control over how shots develop. In practice, these features could also reduce reliance on repeated generations and manual selection, although their effectiveness will depend on the complexity of the scenes being created.

The real challenge of long-form video is more than duration

Kling 4.0 supports native video generation of up to 30 seconds and allows existing videos to be extended, providing more room for continuous action and multi-part storytelling. But longer videos do not automatically make for more complete stories.

According to a Kling AI spokesperson, the biggest technical bottleneck as AI video moves toward longer-form content remains stability, controllability and narrative coherence over extended periods. As video length increases, models must maintain consistency in character identity, spatial relationships, action continuity, camera direction, lighting and audio-visual synchronization.

This is a key challenge for AI video as it moves beyond short clips toward complete productions. A compelling shot lasting a few seconds can be obtained through repeated generation and selection. A longer work, however, requires shots to connect naturally, characters to behave consistently with the storyline, and the visual style to remain coherent throughout.

In this context, Kling 4.0’s upgrades are not simply about extending video duration. They also seek to give creators greater control over the video production process as a whole.

What comes after better-looking AI video?

As the visual quality of AI-generated video improves, comparisons based solely on realism are becoming less sufficient to assess a product’s competitiveness. For professional creators, the ability to reproduce characters consistently, control camera movements, follow storyboards and reduce the cost of repeated revisions is equally important.

A Kling AI spokesperson described this as a natural evolution of the industry. As overall visual quality improves, fidelity is becoming a baseline capability rather than the sole competitive advantage. The next priorities are more precise creative control and a better understanding of scripts and storyboards.

This shift also reflects the practical demands of film and video production. Whether creating advertisements, animation or films, creators need shots that work together to convey a broader narrative, rather than a collection of visually impressive moments. A model’s ability to interpret directorial intent and maintain continuity between shots will influence how useful AI tools are in professional production.

According to a Kling AI spokesperson, the future of AI video tools lies beyond individual generation tasks and will increasingly encompass ideation, reference input, shot generation, editing, video extension and iterative refinement.

More control does not mean AI can independently make a film. Story development, shot selection and final editing still require human judgment. The more important question is whether AI models can give creators enough control and consistency to make the production process more predictable, rather than leaving them to repeatedly generate footage in search of usable results.

For AI video tools, the next test is not simply whether they can generate a convincing shot, but whether they can deliver the right shots, in the right sequence, with enough consistency to serve a larger story. That is what will determine whether AI video can move beyond generating individual clips and become a practical part of filmmaking.

item.title: Robot AI developer Ruoyu secures Pre-A funding led by Sunway Communication
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Shenzhen-based robot AI developer Ruoyu Technology has completed a nine-figure RMB Pre-A funding round led by Sunway Communication, 36Kr reported on October 15. Other investors include Jinmu Capital, Qindao Capital, Huanghai Capital and Zhongchuang Capital. Founded in 2023 and incubated by Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, Ruoyu develops AI systems that help robots perceive environments, […]
item.content:encoded:
Shenzhen-based robot AI developer Ruoyu Technology has completed a nine-figure RMB Pre-A funding round led by Sunway Communication, 36Kr reported on October 15. Other investors include Jinmu Capital, Qindao Capital, Huanghai Capital and Zhongchuang Capital.

Founded in 2023 and incubated by Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, Ruoyu develops AI systems that help robots perceive environments, plan tasks and control physical actions. Its Jiutian robot “brain” combines cloud-based planning with local perception and control.

The company has used robotic refueling as an initial commercial application, testing an explosion-protected system at a station in Foshan. It plans to use the funding to improve its robot AI, collect operational data from real-world deployments and expand commercialization. [36Kr, in Chinese]

item.title: Apple Intelligence to enter China beta testing this month, Tim Cook confirms
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Apple will release a beta version of Apple Intelligence in China later in October, executive chairman Tim Cook confirmed in an interview in Shanghai on October 15. Cook said the initial features and the associated Alibaba Qwen models had received regulatory approval. The first batch will include live translation, writing tools and photo cleanup, while […]
item.content:encoded:
Apple will release a beta version of Apple Intelligence in China later in October, executive chairman Tim Cook confirmed in an interview in Shanghai on October 15. Cook said the initial features and the associated Alibaba Qwen models had received regulatory approval.

The first batch will include live translation, writing tools and photo cleanup, while the redesigned Siri AI assistant will not be included. The announcement provides a timetable for Chinese users to test the service ahead of the December public rollout previously reported by Bloomberg. [The Paper, in Chinese]

item.title: Ant Group open-sources 560-billion-parameter Ling-3.1-flash AI model
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Ant Group has released the weights of Ling-3.1-flash, making its AI model available for developers to deploy on their own infrastructure. The model has approximately 560 billion total parameters, activates about 25 billion per token and supports a context window of up to one million tokens. The release follows the model’s earlier introduction and includes […]
item.content:encoded:
Ant Group has released the weights of Ling-3.1-flash, making its AI model available for developers to deploy on their own infrastructure. The model has approximately 560 billion total parameters, activates about 25 billion per token and supports a context window of up to one million tokens.

The release follows the model’s earlier introduction and includes deployment support through inference frameworks such as SGLang and vLLM. It targets coding, agent workflows and professional tasks that require processing long documents and interacting with external tools.

The team has also developed a mixed-precision deployment approach that reduces model-weight memory requirements from approximately 534GB to 292GB. In its reported Hopper GPU configuration, this reduced the deployment requirement from eight GPUs to four. [Ant Group]

item.title: Smartphone maker Transsion completes Hong Kong listing, raising about HKD 3.06 billion
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Transsion Holdings, the Chinese smartphone maker behind TECNO, Infinix and itel, began trading on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on October 15 under stock code 02636. The company offered approximately 86.65 million H shares at HKD 35.30 each, raising about HKD 3.06 billion before expenses. The Hong Kong listing adds a second capital-market platform alongside […]
item.content:encoded:
Transsion Holdings, the Chinese smartphone maker behind TECNO, Infinix and itel, began trading on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on October 15 under stock code 02636. The company offered approximately 86.65 million H shares at HKD 35.30 each, raising about HKD 3.06 billion before expenses.

The Hong Kong listing adds a second capital-market platform alongside Transsion’s existing Shanghai STAR Market listing, which dates to 2019. The company said the move would broaden funding channels for its global expansion.

Transsion sells products in more than 100 countries and regions. Alongside smartphones, it is expanding accessories, home appliances, energy storage and mobile internet services, while increasing the use of AI in product development and its service ecosystem. [Transsion, in Chinese]

item.title: Desktop manufacturing startup InfiMaker raises tens of millions of dollars in Pre-A+ funding
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Chinese desktop manufacturing startup InfiMaker has completed a Pre-A+ funding round worth tens of millions of dollars from IDG Capital and Kunlun Capital, STAR Market Daily reported on October 15. The company develops compact five-axis computer numerical control machines for professional users and creators. Founded in 2024 by former DJI employees and robotics researchers, InfiMaker […]
item.content:encoded:
Chinese desktop manufacturing startup InfiMaker has completed a Pre-A+ funding round worth tens of millions of dollars from IDG Capital and Kunlun Capital, STAR Market Daily reported on October 15. The company develops compact five-axis computer numerical control machines for professional users and creators.

Founded in 2024 by former DJI employees and robotics researchers, InfiMaker combines machining hardware with its own computer-aided manufacturing software. Its K1 machine coordinates five axes to produce complex shapes, with applications including prototyping, jewelry making, dental work and education.

The K1 raised more than RMB 30 million on Kickstarter, and deliveries are expected to begin by the end of 2026. InfiMaker has established a factory in Shenzhen and will use the new funding and crowdfunding proceeds to scale production, improve its software and expand distribution. [STAR Market Daily, in Chinese]

item.description: XPENG opened presales for its MONA L05 five-seat SUV in China on October 15, with five variants priced between RMB 169,800 and RMB 191,800. The official launch is scheduled for October 29, with both battery-electric and extended-range versions available. The electric versions offer CLTC ranges of 535 or 635 kilometers, while the extended-range versions have […]
item.content:encoded:
XPENG opened presales for its MONA L05 five-seat SUV in China on October 15, with five variants priced between RMB 169,800 and RMB 191,800. The official launch is scheduled for October 29, with both battery-electric and extended-range versions available.

The electric versions offer CLTC ranges of 535 or 635 kilometers, while the extended-range versions have a combined fuel-and-battery range of 1,310 kilometers. Both powertrain options start at RMB 169,800.

The L05 expands MONA’s lineup with a larger SUV positioned above the L03. It features XPENG’s second-generation VLA driver-assistance system, with one Turing AI chip in Max versions and two in Ultra SE versions. XPENG said cumulative deliveries across the MONA series have exceeded 350,000 vehicles. [XPENG, in Chinese]

item.title: Xiaomi open-sources audio AI model that can identify where sounds come from
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Xiaomi has open-sourced MiDashengLM-Spatial, an audio-language model that combines general sound understanding with spatial awareness. The company released model weights and inference code under the Apache 2.0 license. Built on Xiaomi’s MiDashengLM audio model, the system processes binaural audio to identify sound sources and reason about their positions and spatial relationships. It retains capabilities such […]
item.content:encoded:
Xiaomi has open-sourced MiDashengLM-Spatial, an audio-language model that combines general sound understanding with spatial awareness. The company released model weights and inference code under the Apache 2.0 license.

Built on Xiaomi’s MiDashengLM audio model, the system processes binaural audio to identify sound sources and reason about their positions and spatial relationships. It retains capabilities such as speech recognition, audio captioning and questions about environmental sounds and music.

Xiaomi plans to bring the technology to smart-home products and vehicle cabins, enabling devices to respond to both what they hear and where the sound originates. The release extends its Dasheng audio-model series beyond recognizing sound content to understanding the surrounding acoustic environment. [Xiaomi]

item.title: Teaching Robots the Shape of Reality: Hesai’s Kosmo turns real places into 3D assets
item.dc:creator: TechNode Staff
item.description: Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter. Physical AI is moving beyond pre-programmed robots toward systems that can understand, decide, and adapt. But unlike digital AI, which can learn from vast amounts of online data, physical AI faces a shortage of real-world data needed to train models and improve robotic capabilities. […]
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter.

Physical AI is moving beyond pre-programmed robots toward systems that can understand, decide, and adapt. But unlike digital AI, which can learn from vast amounts of online data, physical AI faces a shortage of real-world data needed to train models and improve robotic capabilities.

What happened: At its Kosmo AI Day in Shanghai on Oct. 14, Hesai launched Kosmo, a 3D world data engine designed to transform physical environments into high-fidelity 3D digital spaces for robot training, world model development and immersive content creation.

Why it matters: Kosmo is positioned as data infrastructure for Physical AI, addressing the challenge of obtaining real-world data that is accurate, affordable and available at scale.

How it works: Kosmo captures real spaces with lidar, imaging and motion data, then turns them into 3D scenes with AI-generated completion and object labeling.

  • Kosmo adapts scenes for robot simulation and can generate over 10,000 training trajectories from a single capture.
  • “Physical AI needs infrastructure that lets it understand the real world and act within it,” said Dr. Yifan “David” Li, Hesai’s co-founder and CEO.

In practice: Hesai showcased applications in robotics, film and media, cultural tourism and heritage, and spatial commerce.

  • Robotics: In a Dairy Queen store demo with robot maker Sharpa, a 15-minute Kosmo scan replaced about 300 hours of manual modelling. Sharpa’s robot then achieved a 99% task-success rate in the reconstructed setting.
  • Visual effects: Pixar’s RenderMan tutorial used a Kosmo scan of its campus plaza. The scene contained 1.25 million splats and worked in Houdini and RenderMan.
  • Spatial commerce: Through its Amap partnership, Hesai has brought 3D reconstructions of the Gravity Art Museum and PIFO Gallery to Amap’s “Flying Street View,” with the goal of extending navigation from stores to products inside them.

Ecosystem: Kosmo supports open access to raw capture data and 3D assets, with integrations including NVIDIA Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab, Unreal Engine, RenderMan and Houdini. Hesai offers hardware-and-software solutions as well as spatial-data services and has partnered with Galbot and Dexmal to advance embodied AI.

Zoom out: Digital AI can draw on vast online datasets. Physical AI needs scenes that reflect the geometry and constraints of actual places. Kosmo is one attempt to turn those scenes into reusable assets for simulation and training.
